message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This audit is based on the full appointment record for six months, all 24,860 booked appointments, rather than a sample, so the figures are complete and the rates are exact. We were careful with definitions, separating genuine DNAs from late cancellations, and we costed the impact in clinical time so the Division can see what is at stake: around £80,900 every six months. The most useful finding is about reminder calls. Patients who received a call had a DNA rate of 6.0% against 12.5% for those who did not, which shows that a simple, low-tech intervention the service already uses more than halves missed appointments. Extending it is the obvious, practical step, and it uses staff and processes that are already in place, so it does not need new funding. We also identified concrete, fixable weaknesses in the discharge policy and in refilling late cancellations. I believe the recommendations are proportionate and will bring the service within target.
</author>

The review is to check that the recommendation is clear and the document is ready to go to the decision-makers.

<document>
Internal Audit Memo: Missed Appointments in Outpatient Physiotherapy
To: Director of Operations, Therapies Division
From: Clinical Audit Team
Date: 14 August 2026

1. Scope
This audit examined missed appointments in the outpatient physiotherapy service across our three clinic sites between 1 January and 30 June 2026. For the purposes of this audit, a "did not attend" (DNA) is recorded when a patient fails to attend without giving notice. Late cancellations (less than 24 hours' notice) are recorded and reported separately, because the slot can sometimes be offered to another patient. We reviewed the appointment system records for all 24,860 booked appointments in the period and interviewed reception and clinical staff at each site.

2. Overall position
There were 2,610 DNAs in the period, a DNA rate of 10.5%, against the service target of 8%. Each DNA leaves a 30-minute clinical slot unused. At the service's average cost per clinical hour of £62, the 1,305 lost clinical hours represent around £80,900 of clinical time over six months.

Table 1. DNA rate by appointment type
Appointment type | Booked | DNAs | DNA rate
New patient assessment | 6,210 | 410 | 6.6%
Follow-up | 18,650 | 2,200 | 11.8%
Total | 24,860 | 2,610 | 10.5%

Follow-up appointments account for most DNAs. Staff told us that many patients stop attending once their symptoms improve, without telling the service.

3. Reminder calls
Since 2024, reception staff have phoned patients two working days before their appointment where time allows. In the audit period, staff made reminder calls for 7,800 appointments, about 300 a week over the 26 weeks. A call is recorded as received only if the patient answered and confirmed they would attend; unanswered calls are not recorded. Reception staff estimate that each call, including dialling, rescheduling where needed and updating the record, takes an average of four minutes.

Table 2. DNA rate by reminder status
Reminder status | Appointments | DNAs | DNA rate
Reminder call received | 7,800 | 470 | 6.0%
No reminder call recorded | 17,060 | 2,140 | 12.5%

Patients who received a reminder call were less than half as likely to miss their appointment. Reminder calls therefore more than halve the DNA rate, and extending them to all appointments would bring the service well within its 8% target.

4. Discharge policy
The service's policy is that a patient who DNAs twice without explanation is discharged back to their referrer. We found the policy was applied inconsistently: of 160 patients who met the criterion, 104 were discharged. Staff were reluctant to discharge patients they knew to be vulnerable.

5. Late cancellations
In addition to the DNAs above, 1,140 appointments were cancelled with less than 24 hours' notice. Reception staff were able to refill 31% of these slots, usually with patients on the cancellation list.

6. Findings and recommendations
Finding 1. The DNA rate of 10.5% (including late cancellations, which we classify as DNAs) is above target and costs the service around £80,900 in clinical time every six months.
Recommendation 1. Extend reminder calls to all booked appointments, about 960 a week, using reception staff. This can be absorbed within existing reception hours at no additional cost.

Finding 2. The two-DNA discharge policy is applied inconsistently.
Recommendation 2. Revise the policy to include a documented clinical review before discharge, so that vulnerable patients are protected and the policy can then be applied consistently.

Finding 3. Late-cancellation slots are refilled only 31% of the time.
Recommendation 3. Introduce an automated text offer to patients on the cancellation list when a slot becomes free.

7. Conclusion
Missed appointments are costly but largely preventable. Reminder calls have been shown to more than halve DNAs in this service, and extending them to every patient, together with the policy and process changes above, should bring the DNA rate below target within six months.
</document>
response:
# Review: Missed Appointments in Outpatient Physiotherapy

**Verdict: not ready to go.** The arithmetic checks out, and the discharge and late-cancellation sections are sound. But the headline recommendation rests on a comparison that cannot show what the memo claims. It is also costed in a way the memo's own figures contradict. Finding 1 also contradicts the Scope section about how late cancellations are counted. A Director acting on this would commit roughly 1.5 FTE of reception time to an intervention whose effect is unknown, believing it is free and proven.

## 1. The reminder-call comparison does not show that calls reduce DNAs (critical)

Section 3 says a call is recorded as received "only if the patient answered and confirmed they would attend; unanswered calls are not recorded." So the two groups in Table 2 are:

- **6.0% group:** patients who could be reached and said they would come.
- **12.5% group:** patients never called, *plus* patients who were called but didn't answer, *plus* (presumably) those who answered but didn't confirm.

The first group is pre-selected for engagement. People who pick up and confirm are already more likely to attend, call or no call. People who can't be reached are the most likely to DNA, and they are counted in the comparison group. Calls were also made "where time allows," so who got called was not random. That allocation may also differ by appointment type, site or day.

The gap between 6.0% and 12.5% is therefore some unknown mix of call effect and selection. It could be mostly selection. "Reminder calls therefore more than halve the DNA rate" (Section 3) and "have been shown to more than halve DNAs" (Section 7) are not supported.

The author's point that this uses the full record rather than a sample is true. But completeness makes the rates exact, not unbiased. A full count of a confounded comparison is still confounded. And the reminder data is itself incomplete, because unanswered calls were never logged.

**Suggested fixes:**
- Reword Section 3 to describe an *association* among patients who confirmed attendance, and state the selection problem plainly.
- If the data allow, break Table 2 down by appointment type. Follow-ups DNA at nearly twice the rate of new assessments, so a skew in who gets called could drive part of the gap.
- Replace Recommendation 1 with a **pilot that can measure the effect.** For example, call all appointments at one site, or on alternating weeks, for 8–12 weeks. Log *every* attempt and its outcome. Then compare DNA rates for everyone *offered* a call against everyone not offered one.

## 2. "No additional cost" contradicts the memo's own numbers (critical)

Using the memo's figures:

| | Calls/week | × 4 min | Staff hours/week |
|---|---|---|---|
| Current | 300 | 1,200 min | **20 h** |
| Proposed | 960 | 3,840 min | **64 h** |
| Increase | +660 | +2,640 min | **+44 h (~1.2 FTE)** |

This understates the real load. The 300/week counts only *confirmed* calls, so unanswered dial attempts already add unrecorded time. Extending to all patients would add many more of them.

The service currently calls only "where time allows." That suggests reception has no spare capacity even for 20 hours a week, so it cannot absorb 64. The claim should be removed. Recommendation 1 needs a staffing cost set against the benefit. Automated SMS reminders are worth costing as an alternative. They are far cheaper per contact, and the memo already proposes automated texts in Recommendation 3.

## 3. Finding 1 contradicts the Scope and the figures (must fix)

Finding 1 says the 10.5% rate is "including late cancellations, which we classify as DNAs." That is wrong on both counts:
- Section 1 says late cancellations are recorded and reported **separately**.
- 10.5% is 2,610 ÷ 24,860, which is DNAs only. Adding the 1,140 late cancellations would give 3,750, or **15.1%**.

Delete the parenthetical. Otherwise readers will doubt every other figure, and the author rightly sees careful definitions as a strength of this audit.

## 4. Other points

- **The £80,900 figure** is the value of clinical time, not cash saved. Clinicians may use DNA slots for notes or admin. "Around £80,900 of clinical time" in Section 2 is accurate. "Costs the service" in Finding 1 overstates it slightly, so align the wording.
- **The conclusion's forecast** ("below target within six months") depends entirely on the unproven call effect. Even taking 6.0% at face value, not every patient will answer. Soften it or tie it to the pilot.
- **Recommendation 2** is sensible. The clinical review step will take clinician time, though, so note who does it and roughly how often. At current volumes it is about 160 cases per six months, which is modest.
- **Recommendation 3** would be stronger with a target refill rate and a rough cost for the texting system.

## Arithmetic check

All figures reconcile: the table totals, 10.5%, 6.6%, 11.8%, 6.0%, 12.5%, 1,305 hours × £62 ≈ £80,900, 7,800 ÷ 26 = 300 per week, about 956 appointments a week, and 104 of 160 discharged.

## Bottom line

Before this goes to decision-makers:
1. Reframe the reminder-call result as an association with a selection problem.
2. Turn Recommendation 1 into a measured pilot with honest staffing costs.
3. Correct the late-cancellation line in Finding 1.

The underlying work is good. The problem is that the memo's central claim goes further than its data can support.
